The dataset comprises 25,000 records across 24 features, capturing operational, logistical, and infrastructural attributes of warehouses belonging to the FMCG company. The target variable, product_wg_ton, represents the total weight of product shipped (in tons) over the last three months and contains no missing values. Of the 24 features, 8 are categorical (object type) and 16 are numerical (int64/float64). An initial inspection reveals missing values in three columns: wh_est_year (≈47% missing), workers_num (≈4% missing), and approved_wh_govt_certificate (≈3.6% missing). These will be addressed during the Data Preprocessing phase. Identifier columns Ware_house_ID and WH_Manager_ID carry no predictive value and will be dropped prior to modeling.

Duplicate Check: No duplicate records were found in the dataset, confirming data integrity at the row level.
Missing Value Summary: Three columns contain missing values. The wh_est_year column has the most significant gap, with 11,881 missing entries (approximately 47.5% of records), suggesting that establishment year was either not tracked historically or not recorded for a large portion of warehouses. The workers_num column has 990 missing values (~ 4%), and approved_wh_govt_certificate has 908 missing values (~3.6%). Importantly, the target variable product_wg_ton has no missing values, ensuring no target leakage risk from imputation. These missing values will be treated appropriately in the Data Preprocessing section.
Statistical Summary: The dataset contains a mix of binary indicator variables (flood_impacted, flood_proof, electric_supply, temp_reg_mach) and continuous/count-based numerical features. The target variable product_wg_ton has a mean of approximately 22,103 tons with a standard deviation of 11,608 tons and a range from 2,065 to 55,151 tons, indicating considerable variability in shipment quantities across warehouses — which is precisely the business challenge being addressed. Initial inspection of the interquartile ranges for workers_num, Competitor_in_mkt, transport_issue_l1y, and retail_shop_num suggests the presence of potential outliers, which will be investigated during preprocessing. The identifier columns Ware_house_ID and WH_Manager_ID each have 25,000 unique values and carry no predictive signal; these will be excluded from modeling.

Methodology: Missing values were identified in three columns and treated as follows. For workers_num (990 missing, ~4%), median imputation was applied since the column showed signs of outliers — median is more robust than mean in such cases. For approved_wh_govt_certificate (908 missing, ~3.6%), mode imputation was used as this is a categorical column, with 'C' being the most frequent certification grade. For wh_est_year (11,881 missing, ~47.5%), median imputation was applied using the median year of 2009. While the high missingness rate warrants caution, the column is retained at this stage for further evaluation during feature engineering. Following treatment, all 24 columns report zero missing values, confirming a complete dataset ready for analysis.

Figure 1–6: Distribution of Categorical Features
An analysis of the six categorical features reveals several notable patterns. First, Location_type is heavily skewed, with approximately 91.8% of warehouses located in Rural areas, indicating that the company's supply chain is predominantly structured around rural distribution points. Second, WH_capacity_size shows a near-equal split between Large and Mid-sized warehouses (~ 10,200 and ~ 10,100 respectively), with Small warehouses being fewer (~ 4,800), suggesting the company favors higher-capacity storage infrastructure. Third, the zone distribution reveals a strong concentration in the North zone (~ 10,300 warehouses), with East being severely underrepresented (~ 500 warehouses) — this geographic imbalance may partially explain regional demand-supply mismatches. Fourth, WH_regional_zone shows Zone 6 as the dominant regional zone (~ 8,500), with Zone 1 having the least coverage (~ 2,100). Fifth, wh_owner_type shows a slight majority of Company Owned warehouses (54.3%) over Rented ones (45.7%), which has implications for operational control and cost structure. Finally, approved_wh_govt_certificate reveals that Grade C — the lowest certification tier — is the most prevalent (~6,700 warehouses), raising questions about overall warehouse quality standards and its potential impact on product storage and shipment reliability.

Figure 7: Distribution of Product Shipment Quantity (product_wg_ton) The target variable product_wg_ton exhibits a multimodal distribution with a right skew, ranging from 2,065 to 55,151 tons and a mean of approximately 22,103 tons. Multiple peaks are visible at roughly 5,000–8,000, 18,000, 25,000, and 30,000–32,000 tons, suggesting that warehouses naturally cluster into distinct shipment tiers. This pattern is likely driven by warehouse capacity categories (Small, Mid, Large), where each size class tends to receive systematically different shipment volumes. The right skew indicates a smaller number of high-volume warehouses pulling the mean upward. From a business perspective, this variability confirms that a one-size-fits-all shipment strategy is inappropriate — the model must account for warehouse-level characteristics to predict optimal quantities accurately.

Figure 8: Boxplots of dist_from_hub, workers_num, and num_refill_req_l3m
Among the first group of numerical features, dist_from_hub shows a clean, symmetric distribution ranging from 55 to 271 km with a median of approximately 164 km and no outliers, indicating consistent geographical spread of warehouses from the production hub. num_refill_req_l3m is also clean, ranging from 0 to 8 refill requests with a median of 4, suggesting relatively stable restocking patterns across warehouses. However, workers_num shows a tight IQR of 24–33 with several outliers extending up to 98 workers, indicating that while most warehouses operate with a similar workforce size, a small number of warehouses are significantly larger in terms of staffing.


Figure 9: Boxplots of Remaining Numerical Features
Among the remaining seven numerical features, distributor_num, storage_issue_reported_l3m, wh_breakdown_l3m, and govt_check_l3m all exhibit clean distributions with no significant outliers, suggesting consistent operational patterns across these dimensions. In contrast, transport_issue_l1y shows outliers at values 3, 4, and 5, as most warehouses report 0–1 transport incidents annually, making higher values statistically extreme. Competitor_in_mkt displays outliers above 7, with an IQR of 2–4, reflecting a small number of warehouses operating in unusually high-competition markets. Most notably, retail_shop_num exhibits severe outliers on both ends — above approximately 7,500 and below 2,000 — indicating extreme variation in the retail density served by different warehouses. These four columns — workers_num, transport_issue_l1y, Competitor_in_mkt, and retail_shop_num — will require outlier treatment during the Data Preprocessing phase.

Figure 10: Average Shipment Volume by Zone and Warehouse Capacity
The grouped bar chart reveals that average shipment volumes are broadly consistent across all four zones, ranging between approximately 21,000 and 24,000 tons. The East zone exhibits the highest average for Large warehouses (~24,000 tons) and also shows the most pronounced difference between capacity sizes, suggesting that warehouse size plays a more significant role in determining shipment quantities in the East. In contrast, the North, South, and West zones show near-uniform averages across all three capacity categories, indicating that zone and warehouse capacity alone may not be strong individual predictors of shipment volume. Notably, in the West zone, Mid-sized warehouses slightly outperform Large ones — an anomaly that may reflect local demand dynamics or operational efficiency differences. From a business perspective, these findings suggest that simply expanding warehouse capacity in a given zone may not automatically lead to proportionally higher shipments — other operational factors likely play a significant role.

Figure 11: Scatter Plot — Distance from Hub vs. Shipment Volume
The scatter plot between dist_from_hub and product_wg_ton reveals no meaningful linear relationship between the two variables, as evidenced by the near-horizontal trend line. Shipment volumes are widely and uniformly distributed across the entire distance range of 55 to 271 km, indicating that warehouses receive similar quantities regardless of their proximity to the production hub. From a business perspective, this is a noteworthy finding — it suggests that transportation distance is not currently influencing supply allocation decisions. Ideally, logistics costs associated with greater distances should be factored into shipment planning, as shipping equal quantities to far-flung warehouses incurs disproportionately higher costs. This insight presents an opportunity for the company to incorporate distance-based cost optimization into its supply chain strategy.

From a business standpoint, investing in warehouse quality upgrades could directly translate into higher shipment allocations and improved supply chain reliability.

Figure 14: Distribution of Shipment Volume Across Key Categorical Features
The three boxplots reveal that zone and warehouse capacity size have minimal independent influence on shipment volume. All four geographic zones show nearly identical median shipments of approximately 22,000–23,000 tons with overlapping IQRs, confirming that supply allocation is not systematically differentiated by region. Similarly, Large, Mid, and Small warehouses show almost identical distributions, suggesting warehouse size alone does not drive how much product is allocated. Location type shows a modest difference — Urban warehouses have a slightly higher median (~25,000 tons) and a compressed lower tail compared to Rural, indicating that urban locations may receive marginally higher and more consistent allocations. However, the overall spread in all three panels is wide, pointing to other operational factors being the true drivers of shipment volume.

Figure 15: Warehouse Breakdowns vs Shipment Volume
The scatter plot reveals a clear step-change pattern: warehouses with zero breakdowns in the last three months are confined to a narrow, low-volume band (roughly 2,000–15,000 tons), while warehouses with two or more breakdowns span the full range up to 55,000 tons. This strongly suggests that breakdown frequency is a proxy for operational intensity — high-volume warehouses handle more throughput and consequently experience more operational strain. The relationship is not causal (breakdowns do not increase shipments), but wh_breakdown_l3m is evidently a reliable signal of which warehouses are operating at high capacity, which explains its dominant position in the XGBoost feature importance ranking.

def cap_outliers(df, column):
    Q1 = df[column].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = df[column].quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

    before = ((df[column] < lower) | (df[column] > upper)).sum()
    df[column] = df[column].clip(lower, upper)
    after = ((df[column] < lower) | (df[column] > upper)).sum()

    print(f"{column}:")
    print(f"  Outliers before capping: {before}")
    print(f"  Lower fence: {lower:.2f} | Upper fence: {upper:.2f}")
    print(f"  Outliers after capping: {after}")
    print()

outlier_cols = ['workers_num', 'transport_issue_l1y',
                'Competitor_in_mkt', 'retail_shop_num']

for col in outlier_cols:
    cap_outliers(df, col)
workers_num: Outliers before capping: 607 Lower fence: 10.50 | Upper fence: 46.50 Outliers after capping: 0 transport_issue_l1y: Outliers before capping: 2943 Lower fence: -1.50 | Upper fence: 2.50 Outliers after capping: 0 Competitor_in_mkt: Outliers before capping: 96 Lower fence: -1.00 | Upper fence: 7.00 Outliers after capping: 0 retail_shop_num: Outliers before capping: 948 Lower fence: 2532.50 | Upper fence: 7280.50 Outliers after capping: 0
 
Methodology: Outlier detection was performed visually using boxplots with whiskers set at 1.5×IQR, followed by quantitative confirmation using the IQR method. Values falling below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR were flagged as outliers. Treatment was applied using IQR Capping (Winsorization), where outlying values are capped at the respective lower and upper fences rather than removed — this preserves all 25,000 rows while eliminating the distorting effect of extreme values.
Four columns were identified as containing outliers and treated as follows. workers_num had 607 outliers capped between a lower fence of 10.50 and an upper fence of 46.50, addressing the small number of unusually large warehouse operations identified during univariate analysis. transport_issue_l1y had the highest count of 2,943 outliers capped at an upper fence of 2.50, reflecting that while most warehouses report 0–1 transport incidents annually, a significant number reported higher values that were statistically extreme. Competitor_in_mkt had 96 outliers capped at an upper fence of 7.00, handling the small number of warehouses operating in unusually high-competition markets. Finally, retail_shop_num had 948 outliers capped between 2,532.50 and 7,280.50, addressing the extreme variation in retail density observed during EDA. Following treatment, all four columns report zero remaining outliers, resulting in a cleaner dataset for modeling.

Methodology: One new feature was engineered from the existing dataset. The column wh_est_year was transformed into warehouse_age by subtracting the establishment year from the current year (2026). This transformation serves two purposes — first, it converts an abstract year value into an operationally meaningful metric representing how many years of experience a warehouse has accumulated; second, it reduces the scale of the variable from a large year value (~1996–2023) to a compact range of 3–30 years, which is more suitable for linear regression. Warehouses range from 3 to 30 years old with a mean age of approximately 16.80 years. The original wh_est_year column was dropped following this transformation, maintaining the total column count at 22.

Methodology: Six categorical columns were encoded prior to modeling. Label encoding was applied to four columns with either ordinal or binary nature. WH_capacity_size was mapped ordinally as Small=0, Mid=1, Large=2, preserving the natural size hierarchy. approved_wh_govt_certificate was mapped ordinally as A+=5, A=4, B=2, B+=3, C=1, reflecting the descending quality order. Binary columns Location_type (Urban=1, Rural=0) and wh_owner_type (Company Owned=1, Rented=0) were mapped directly. One-hot encoding with drop_first=True was applied to zone and WH_regional_zone since these are nominal variables with no inherent ranking — drop_first avoids multicollinearity by dropping one reference category from each. This expanded the dataset from 21 to 27 columns.

Methodology: The dataset was split into training and test sets using an 80-20 ratio, resulting in 20,000 training samples and 5,000 test samples across 26 features. A fixed random_state=42 was used to ensure reproducibility. Feature scaling was then applied using StandardScaler, which transforms each feature to have a mean of approximately 0 and a standard deviation of 1. The scaler was fitted exclusively on the training data to prevent data leakage, and the learned parameters were subsequently applied to transform the test set. This ensures that the model's evaluation on the test set genuinely reflects performance on unseen data. Scaling is particularly important for Linear Regression as features with larger scales — such as retail_shop_num (thousands) — would otherwise dominate features with smaller scales such as binary indicators.

import statsmodels.api as sm
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

# Add constant (intercept) to both train and test
X_train_sm = sm.add_constant(X_train_scaled)
X_test_sm = sm.add_constant(X_test_scaled)

# Reset indices of y_train and y_test to align with X_train_sm and X_test_sm
y_train_reset = y_train.reset_index(drop=True)
y_test_reset = y_test.reset_index(drop=True)

# Build Linear Regression model
model = sm.OLS(y_train_reset, X_train_sm).fit()

# Predictions
y_pred_train = model.predict(X_train_sm)
y_pred_test = model.predict(X_test_sm)

# Performance metrics
print("=== TRAINING SET PERFORMANCE ===")
print(f"R²:   {r2_score(y_train_reset, y_pred_train):.4f}")
print(f"RMSE: {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train_reset, y_pred_train)):.2f}")
print(f"MAE:  {mean_absolute_error(y_train_reset, y_pred_train):.2f}")

print("\n=== TEST SET PERFORMANCE ===")
print(f"R²:   {r2_score(y_test_reset, y_pred_test):.4f}")
print(f"RMSE: {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test_reset, y_pred_test)):.2f}")
print(f"MAE:  {mean_absolute_error(y_test_reset, y_pred_test):.2f}")

# Model summary
print("\n=== MODEL SUMMARY ===")
print(model.summary())

Metric of Choice: R² (R-squared)
For this regression problem, R² was selected as the primary evaluation metric as it directly quantifies the proportion of variance in shipment quantity explained by the model — making it intuitively interpretable for business stakeholders. Supporting metrics RMSE and MAE were also computed; RMSE is particularly valuable as it is expressed in the same unit as the target variable (tons), making prediction errors directly actionable for supply chain planning.
Methodology: A baseline Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Linear Regression model was built using statsmodels with an intercept term added via sm.add_constant(). The model was trained on 20,000 samples and evaluated on a held-out test set of 5,000 samples.
Model Performance:
The baseline Linear Regression model achieved an R² of 0.45 on both the training and test sets, indicating that approximately 45% of the variance in warehouse shipment quantities is explained by the selected features. The near-identical performance on training (R²=0.4526, RMSE=8,595 tons, MAE=6,776 tons) and test sets (R²=0.4546, RMSE=8,543 tons, MAE=6,744 tons) confirms that the model is not overfitting and generalises reasonably well to unseen data. The F-statistic of 635.1 with a p-value of 0.00 confirms that the model is statistically significant overall.
Significant Predictors: Among the 26 features, warehouse_age emerged as the strongest predictor (coefficient: 6,318), confirming that older, more established warehouses handle significantly higher shipment volumes. transport_issue_l1y showed a strong negative relationship (coefficient: -2,261), indicating that warehouses with frequent transport disruptions receive less product. approved_wh_govt_certificate (coefficient: 1,284) and wh_breakdown_l3m (coefficient: 1,884) were also significant. Several features including WH_capacity_size, dist_from_hub, workers_num, and all zone-based columns showed no statistically significant relationship with shipment volume at baseline.
Interpretation: While the baseline model provides a reasonable starting point with consistent train-test performance, an R² of 0.45 leaves considerable room for improvement. The 55% unexplained variance suggests that non-linear relationships and feature interactions exist in the data that a simple linear model cannot capture — motivating the use of advanced models in the next phase.

The preprocessing pipeline has been corrected to eliminate data leakage: the train-test split is now performed before any statistical fitting (imputation parameters, outlier fences). wh_est_year has been dropped due to 47.52% missingness which caused a severe imputation spike at 2009, biasing the strongest predictor. All previous interim cells are retained above for reference.

# ── CELL F1: Fresh load, initial cleaning, and train-test split ──────────────
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Re-load original data fresh so this section is self-contained
df_final = pd.read_csv('/content/drive/MyDrive/CSV/supply_chain_data.csv')

print("Original shape:", df_final.shape)

# 1. Drop identifier columns (no predictive value)
df_final.drop(columns=['Ware_house_ID', 'WH_Manager_ID'], inplace=True)

# 2. Drop data leakage column (Pearson r=0.99 with target, confirmed derived variable)
df_final.drop(columns=['storage_issue_reported_l3m'], inplace=True)

# 3. Drop wh_est_year — 47.52% missing; median imputation created ~12k identical

# 4. Separate features and target

y = df_final['product_wg_ton']

# 5. Train-test split FIRST — before any statistical fitting

# ── CELL F3: IQR outlier capping — fences fitted on train set only ───────────

cols_to_cap = ['workers_num', 'transport_issue_l1y', 'Competitor_in_mkt', 'retail_shop_num']

# Store fences fitted on train
fences = {}
for col in cols_to_cap:
    Q1 = X_train[col].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = X_train[col].quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
    fences[col] = (lower, upper)
    print(f"{col}: fences [{lower:.2f}, {upper:.2f}]")

# Apply same fences to both train and test
for col in cols_to_cap:
    lower, upper = fences[col]
    X_train[col] = X_train[col].clip(lower, upper)
    X_test[col]  = X_test[col].clip(lower, upper)

# Verify no outliers remain in train
print("\nOutliers remaining in X_train after capping:")
for col in cols_to_cap:
    lower, upper = fences[col]
    n = ((X_train[col] < lower) | (X_train[col] > upper)).sum()
    print(f"  {col}: {n}")

# ── CELL F4: Categorical encoding and feature scaling ────────────────────────
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# --- Ordinal encoding (preserving natural rank order) ---
X_train['WH_capacity_size'] = X_train['WH_capacity_size'].map({'Small': 0, 'Mid': 1, 'Large': 2})
X_test['WH_capacity_size']  = X_test['WH_capacity_size'].map({'Small': 0, 'Mid': 1, 'Large': 2})

X_train['approved_wh_govt_certificate'] = X_train['approved_wh_govt_certificate'].map(
    {'C': 1, 'B': 2, 'B+': 3, 'A': 4, 'A+': 5})
X_test['approved_wh_govt_certificate']  = X_test['approved_wh_govt_certificate'].map(
    {'C': 1, 'B': 2, 'B+': 3, 'A': 4, 'A+': 5})

# --- Binary encoding ---
X_train['Location_type'] = X_train['Location_type'].map({'Urban': 1, 'Rural': 0})
X_test['Location_type']  = X_test['Location_type'].map({'Urban': 1, 'Rural': 0})

X_train['wh_owner_type'] = X_train['wh_owner_type'].map({'Company Owned': 1, 'Rented': 0})
X_test['wh_owner_type']  = X_test['wh_owner_type'].map({'Company Owned': 1, 'Rented': 0})

# --- One-hot encoding for nominal columns (drop_first avoids dummy variable trap) ---
X_train = pd.get_dummies(X_train, columns=['zone', 'WH_regional_zone'], drop_first=True)
X_test  = pd.get_dummies(X_test,  columns=['zone', 'WH_regional_zone'], drop_first=True)

# Align columns — ensure test has same columns as train (same order)
X_test = X_test.reindex(columns=X_train.columns, fill_value=0)

# Convert any boolean dummy columns to int
for df in [X_train, X_test]:
    bool_cols = df.select_dtypes(include='bool').columns
    df[bool_cols] = df[bool_cols].astype(int)

print("X_train shape after encoding:", X_train.shape)
print("X_test shape after encoding :", X_test.shape)
print("Columns:", X_train.columns.tolist())

# --- Feature scaling: fit on train only, apply to both ---
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = pd.DataFrame(scaler.fit_transform(X_train), columns=X_train.columns)
X_test_scaled  = pd.DataFrame(scaler.transform(X_test),      columns=X_train.columns)

# Reset target indices to align with scaled arrays
y_train = y_train.reset_index(drop=True)
y_test  = y_test.reset_index(drop=True)

print("\nScaling complete.")
print(f"Final feature count: {X_train_scaled.shape[1]}")

Note on Metric Selection — Revision from Interim Submission


The primary evaluation metric has been revised from R² (used in the interim report)
to RMSE for the final submission.

Rationale: RMSE is expressed in the same unit as the target variable (tons),
making prediction errors directly interpretable to operations teams. An RMSE of
10,000 tons means the model's quarterly shipment forecast deviates from actual
demand by 10,000 tons on average — a figure that maps directly to inventory
planning and logistics decisions. R² and MAE are reported alongside RMSE
throughout for completeness.

# ── CELL F5: Baseline OLS Linear Regression — corrected pipeline ─────────────
import statsmodels.api as sm
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score

# Add constant (intercept) term
X_train_sm = sm.add_constant(X_train_scaled)
X_test_sm  = sm.add_constant(X_test_scaled)

# Fit OLS on training set
ols_model = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_sm).fit()

# Predictions
y_pred_train_ols = ols_model.predict(X_train_sm)
y_pred_test_ols  = ols_model.predict(X_test_sm)

# Metrics
def evaluate(y_true, y_pred, label):
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))
    mae  = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
    r2   = r2_score(y_true, y_pred)
    print(f"  {label}  →  RMSE: {rmse:,.2f} tons  |  MAE: {mae:,.2f} tons  |  R²: {r2:.4f}")
    return rmse, mae, r2

print("=== BASELINE OLS LINEAR REGRESSION ===")
train_metrics = evaluate(y_train, y_pred_train_ols, "Train")
test_metrics  = evaluate(y_test,  y_pred_test_ols,  "Test ")

print(f"\n  RMSE gap (train - test): {train_metrics[0] - test_metrics[0]:,.2f} tons")
print(f"  R² gap  (train - test): {train_metrics[2] - test_metrics[2]:.4f}")

print("\n=== SIGNIFICANT PREDICTORS (p < 0.05) ===")
summary_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'coef'   : ols_model.params,
    'pvalue' : ols_model.pvalues
})
sig = summary_df[summary_df['pvalue'] < 0.05].drop('const').sort_values('coef', key=abs, ascending=False)
print(sig.to_string())
# ── CELL F5b: Full OLS summary output ───────────────────────────────────────
print(ols_model.summary())

Corrected Baseline Model Performance
Following pipeline correction — split-first preprocessing and removal of wh_est_year — the OLS baseline achieves a test RMSE of 10,379 tons and R² of 0.19. The near-zero gap between train and test performance (RMSE gap: 105 tons; R² gap: 0.009) confirms the model generalises cleanly with no overfitting.
The reduction in R² compared to the interim report (0.45 → 0.19) is expected and represents honest model performance. The interim figure was inflated by warehouse_age, a feature derived from a column with 47.52% missing values, where median imputation assigned ~12,000 records an identical value of 17 years. Removing it eliminates this bias at the cost of explanatory power — a sound trade-off that the advanced non-linear models are expected to recover through feature interactions.
Five predictors remain statistically significant at p < 0.05: wh_breakdown_l3m (+3,580 tons), transport_issue_l1y (−2,170 tons), approved_wh_govt_certificate (+1,889 per grade step), Location_type (+717 tons for urban), and temp_reg_mach (+489 tons). This corrected baseline sets the performance floor: test RMSE of 10,379 tons is the benchmark all advanced models must beat.

# ── CELL F6: Advanced models — all 6, default parameters ────────────────────
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import (BaggingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor,
                               AdaBoostRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor)
from xgboost import XGBRegressor
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

# For tree-based models we use unscaled data (trees don't need scaling)
# Reset indices to be safe
X_tr = X_train.reset_index(drop=True)
X_te = X_test.reset_index(drop=True)

models = {
    'Decision Tree'      : DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42),
    'Bagging'            : BaggingRegressor(random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    'Random Forest'      : RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    'AdaBoost'           : AdaBoostRegressor(random_state=42),
    'Gradient Boosting'  : GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=42),
    'XGBoost'            : XGBRegressor(random_state=42, n_jobs=-1,
                                        verbosity=0, eval_metric='rmse'),
}

results = []

for name, model in models.items():
    model.fit(X_tr, y_train)

    y_pred_tr = model.predict(X_tr)
    y_pred_te = model.predict(X_te)

    tr_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, y_pred_tr))
    te_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test,  y_pred_te))
    tr_mae  = mean_absolute_error(y_train, y_pred_tr)
    te_mae  = mean_absolute_error(y_test,  y_pred_te)
    tr_r2   = r2_score(y_train, y_pred_tr)
    te_r2   = r2_score(y_test,  y_pred_te)

    results.append({
        'Model'       : name,
        'Train RMSE'  : round(tr_rmse, 2),
        'Test RMSE'   : round(te_rmse, 2),
        'Train MAE'   : round(tr_mae, 2),
        'Test MAE'    : round(te_mae, 2),
        'Train R²'    : round(tr_r2, 4),
        'Test R²'     : round(te_r2, 4),
        'RMSE Gap'    : round(tr_rmse - te_rmse, 2),
    })
    print(f"✓ {name} done")

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values('Test RMSE')
print("\n=== ADVANCED MODELS — DEFAULT PARAMETERS ===")
print(results_df.to_string(index=False))

Advanced Models — Default Parameter Performance
All six models were trained on unscaled data (tree-based models are invariant to feature scaling) using default hyperparameters to establish pre-tuning benchmarks. Results are summarised in Table X below, sorted by test RMSE.
Gradient Boosting delivers the best test RMSE of 9,909 tons with a near-zero train-test gap of 39 tons, indicating strong generalisation. AdaBoost follows with a test RMSE of 10,077 tons and a gap of 164 tons — also well-controlled. Both boosting methods outperform the corrected OLS baseline (10,379 tons).
Random Forest and Bagging exhibit severe overfitting at default settings: train RMSE of 3,830 and 4,513 tons respectively against test RMSE above 10,000 tons, with negative RMSE gaps of ~6,000 tons. This is caused by unconstrained tree depth — individual trees perfectly memorise the training data. Decision Tree is the most extreme case, achieving perfect train fit (R²=1.00, RMSE=0) but collapsing on test data (RMSE: 14,391 tons; R²: −0.55), confirming complete overfitting. XGBoost at default parameters performs below the OLS baseline on the test set, suggesting it requires tuning to unlock its potential on this dataset.
Three models are selected for hyperparameter tuning: Gradient Boosting (best test performance), Random Forest (high variance suggesting regularisation will help significantly), and XGBoost (known to improve substantially with tuning).

# ── CELL F7: Hyperparameter tuning — Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, XGBoost
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor
from xgboost import XGBRegressor
import time

X_tr = X_train.reset_index(drop=True)
X_te = X_test.reset_index(drop=True)

# ── 1. Gradient Boosting ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
gb_params = {
    'n_estimators'    : [100, 200, 300],
    'learning_rate'   : [0.05, 0.1, 0.2],
    'max_depth'       : [3, 4, 5],
    'min_samples_leaf': [10, 20, 30],
    'subsample'       : [0.7, 0.8, 1.0],
}
gb_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=42),
    gb_params, n_iter=30, cv=5, scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error',
    random_state=42, n_jobs=-1, verbose=1
)
t0 = time.time()
gb_search.fit(X_tr, y_train)
print(f"GB tuning done in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s | Best params: {gb_search.best_params_}")

# ── 2. Random Forest ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rf_params = {
    'n_estimators'    : [100, 200, 300],
    'max_depth'       : [10, 20, 30, None],
    'min_samples_leaf': [10, 20, 40],
    'max_features'    : ['sqrt', 'log2', 0.5],
}
rf_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42, n_jobs=-1),
    rf_params, n_iter=30, cv=5, scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error',
    random_state=42, n_jobs=-1, verbose=1
)
t0 = time.time()
rf_search.fit(X_tr, y_train)
print(f"RF tuning done in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s | Best params: {rf_search.best_params_}")

# ── 3. XGBoost ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
xgb_params = {
    'n_estimators'  : [100, 200, 300],
    'learning_rate' : [0.05, 0.1, 0.2],
    'max_depth'     : [3, 4, 6],
    'subsample'     : [0.7, 0.8, 1.0],
    'colsample_bytree': [0.7, 0.8, 1.0],
    'reg_alpha'     : [0, 0.1, 1.0],
}
xgb_search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    XGBRegressor(random_state=42, n_jobs=-1, verbosity=0, eval_metric='rmse'),

)
t0 = time.time()
xgb_search.fit(X_tr, y_train)
print(f"XGB tuning done in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s | Best params: {xgb_search.best_params_}")

print("\n=== BEST PARAMETERS SUMMARY ===")
print("Gradient Boosting:", gb_search.best_params_)
print("Random Forest    :", rf_search.best_params_)
print("XGBoost          :", xgb_search.best_params_)

# ── CELL F8: Evaluate tuned models on train and test sets ────────────────────

tuned_models = {
    'Gradient Boosting (Tuned)': gb_search.best_estimator_,
    'Random Forest (Tuned)'    : rf_search.best_estimator_,
    'XGBoost (Tuned)'          : xgb_search.best_estimator_,
}

tuned_results = []

for name, model in tuned_models.items():
    y_pred_tr = model.predict(X_tr)
    y_pred_te = model.predict(X_te)

    tr_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_train, y_pred_tr))
    te_rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test,  y_pred_te))
    tr_mae  = mean_absolute_error(y_train, y_pred_tr)
    te_mae  = mean_absolute_error(y_test,  y_pred_te)
    tr_r2   = r2_score(y_train, y_pred_tr)
    te_r2   = r2_score(y_test,  y_pred_te)

    tuned_results.append({
        'Model'      : name,
        'Train RMSE' : round(tr_rmse, 2),
        'Test RMSE'  : round(te_rmse, 2),
        'Train MAE'  : round(tr_mae, 2),
        'Test MAE'   : round(te_mae, 2),
        'Train R²'   : round(tr_r2, 4),
        'Test R²'    : round(te_r2, 4),
        'RMSE Gap'   : round(tr_rmse - te_rmse, 2),
    })
    print(f"✓ {name}")
    print(f"   Train → RMSE: {tr_rmse:,.2f} | MAE: {tr_mae:,.2f} | R²: {tr_r2:.4f}")
    print(f"   Test  → RMSE: {te_rmse:,.2f} | MAE: {te_mae:,.2f} | R²: {te_r2:.4f}")
    print(f"   RMSE Gap: {tr_rmse - te_rmse:,.2f}\n")

tuned_df = pd.DataFrame(tuned_results).sort_values('Test RMSE')
print("=== TUNED MODELS COMPARISON ===")
print(tuned_df.to_string(index=False))

Section 5 — Model Building: Advanced Models (Report Write-up)


5.1 Methodology


Six advanced models were trained on unscaled data using default hyperparameters to establish pre-tuning benchmarks: Decision Tree, Bagging, Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost. Tree-based models are invariant to feature scaling, so the unscaled encoded dataset was used directly. All models were evaluated on the same 80/20 train-test split using RMSE as the primary metric.

5.2 Model Performance — Default Parameters


Table 10: Advanced Models — Default Parameter Performance

| Model | Train RMSE | Test RMSE | Train R² | Test R² | RMSE Gap |
|-------|-----------|----------|---------|--------|---------|
| Gradient Boosting | 9,948.55 | 9,909.22 | 0.2667 | 0.2661 | 39.33 |
| AdaBoost | 10,240.98 | 10,076.94 | 0.2229 | 0.2411 | 164.04 |
| Random Forest | 3,829.51 | 10,152.37 | 0.8913 | 0.2297 | −6,322.86 |
| XGBoost | 7,657.39 | 10,352.70 | 0.5656 | 0.1990 | −2,695.31 |
| Bagging | 4,513.42 | 10,596.95 | 0.8491 | 0.1607 | −6,083.53 |
| Decision Tree | 0.00 | 14,390.93 | 1.0000 | −0.5478 | −14,390.93 |

Gradient Boosting delivers the best test RMSE at default settings (9,909 tons), with a near-zero train-test gap of just 39 tons — indicating excellent generalisation without any tuning. AdaBoost is second with a test RMSE of 10,077 tons and a controlled gap of 164 tons. Both boosting methods outperform the corrected OLS baseline (10,379 tons) immediately.

Random Forest and Bagging exhibit severe overfitting at defaults — train RMSE of 3,830 and 4,513 tons respectively, against test RMSE above 10,000 tons. This is caused by unconstrained tree depth where individual trees memorise the training data perfectly. Decision Tree is the most extreme case: perfect train fit (R²=1.00, RMSE=0) but complete collapse on test data (RMSE: 14,391 tons; R²: −0.55), confirming total overfitting. XGBoost at default parameters performs below the OLS baseline on the test set, indicating it requires tuning to unlock its potential on this dataset.

---

Section 6 — Hyperparameter Tuning (Report Write-up)


6.1 Model Selection for Tuning


Three models were selected for hyperparameter tuning based on the following reasoning:

Gradient Boosting — best default test performance and near-zero overfitting gap. Tuning is expected to further reduce RMSE by optimising the learning rate and tree depth interaction.

Random Forest — large train-test gap (~6,300 tons) indicates the model has high variance that can be substantially reduced through depth constraints and feature subsampling. High upside from regularisation.

XGBoost — known to improve dramatically with tuning. Its default performance below the OLS baseline strongly suggests the default hyperparameters are poorly suited to this dataset's structure, and tuning will unlock its capacity.

AdaBoost was not selected as it already performs well at defaults with limited hyperparameter surface to optimise. Decision Tree and Bagging were not selected due to their fundamental overfitting behaviour at defaults.

6.2 Tuning Methodology


RandomizedSearchCV with 5-fold cross-validation was used for all three models, with n_iter=30 random combinations per model (150 total fits per model; 450 total across all three). Scoring was set to neg_root_mean_squared_error to directly optimise the primary metric. The search grids covered key regularisation parameters for each model family.

Best parameters found:

| Model | Best Parameters |
|-------|----------------|
| Gradient Boosting | n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=5, min_samples_leaf=30, subsample=0.8 |
| Random Forest | n_estimators=200, max_depth=10, min_samples_leaf=20, max_features=0.5 |
| XGBoost | n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=4, subsample=1.0, colsample_bytree=1.0, reg_alpha=0 |

6.3 Tuned Model Performance


Table 11: Tuned Model Performance

| Model | Train RMSE | Test RMSE | Train MAE | Test MAE | Train R² | Test R² | RMSE Gap |
|-------|-----------|----------|----------|---------|---------|--------|---------|
| XGBoost (Tuned) | 9,951.81 | 9,896.62 | 7,981.74 | 7,922.19 | 0.2662 | 0.2680 | 55.19 |
| Gradient Boosting (Tuned) | 9,822.43 | 9,904.62 | 7,870.10 | 7,932.17 | 0.2852 | 0.2668 | −82.19 |
| Random Forest (Tuned) | 9,599.28 | 9,914.08 | 7,676.47 | 7,931.01 | 0.3173 | 0.2654 | −314.81 |

All three tuned models achieve test RMSE within 18 tons of each other — a remarkably tight cluster that confirms the dataset's inherent predictive ceiling with the available features. Tuning successfully eliminated the overfitting in Random Forest (gap reduced from −6,323 to −315 tons). XGBoost improved from 10,353 to 9,897 tons on the test set — a 456-ton gain purely from tuning.

---

Section 7 — Model Comparison and Final Model Selection (Report Write-up)


7.1 Complete Model Comparison


Table 12: Complete Model Performance Summary — All Models

| XGBoost (Tuned) | 9,896.62 | 7,922.19 | 0.2680 | 55.19 | Best |

7.2 Final Model Selection — XGBoost (Tuned)


XGBoost (Tuned) is selected as the final model on three grounds. First, it achieves the lowest test RMSE (9,896.62 tons) across all 10 models evaluated. Second, it has the highest test R² (0.2680) and lowest test MAE (7,922.19 tons). Third, its RMSE gap of just 55 tons is the most controlled among the tuned models, confirming robust generalisation to unseen warehouses.

Compared to the corrected OLS baseline, the final model reduces test RMSE by 482.79 tons (a 4.7% improvement). While modest in percentage terms, at the scale of a 25,000-warehouse national network this translates to meaningfully more accurate quarterly shipment forecasts. The overall R² of 0.27 reflects the genuine difficulty of this prediction task — the majority of shipment variance is driven by non-linear interactions and features not captured in the available dataset, which the advanced models partially but not fully resolve.

---

Section 8 — Actionable Insights & Recommendations (Report Write-up)


8.1 Key Insights from the Analysis


Insight 1 — Warehouse breakdowns are the single strongest predictor of shipment volume. XGBoost's feature importance analysis shows wh_breakdown_l3m accounts for 52% of total predictive importance — far exceeding all other features combined. This is a positive association: higher-volume warehouses experience more operational strain and therefore more breakdowns. It is not that breakdowns cause higher shipments, but that breakdown frequency is a proxy for operational intensity.

Insight 2 — Transport reliability is the strongest controllable negative driver. transport_issue_l1y ranks second in importance (~10%). The OLS baseline quantifies this at −2,170 tons per incident — every transport disruption directly reduces the quarterly allocation a warehouse receives. This is the most actionable lever in the model.

Insight 3 — Government certification grade has a strong positive effect. approved_wh_govt_certificate ranks third (~9% importance; +1,889 tons per grade step in OLS). Upgrading from Grade C to Grade A+ (four steps) is associated with approximately 7,500 additional tons per quarter — roughly 30,000 tons annually per warehouse.

Insight 4 — Cold-chain capability and urban location provide consistent advantages. Temperature regulation machinery and urban location type both appear consistently significant across the OLS model and feature importance rankings, suggesting that infrastructure investment and location strategy both influence supply allocation.

Insight 5 — Geographic zone and warehouse capacity do not independently drive allocation. Zone dummy variables and warehouse capacity size rank near the bottom of the feature importance chart and were not significant in OLS. The current supply model does not systematically differentiate by region or size — a finding that represents both a gap and an opportunity.

Insight 6 — The overall R² of ~0.27 signals missing predictors. Approximately 73% of shipment variance remains unexplained by the available features. Variables such as actual local consumer demand, seasonal patterns, promotional activity, and competitor pricing — none of which are present in the dataset — are likely the true primary drivers of shipment volume at the warehouse level.

8.2 Business Recommendations


Recommendation 1 — Invest in transport risk management immediately. At −2,170 tons per incident, transport disruptions are the most directly controllable cost in the supply chain. The company should implement route diversification, carrier performance standards, real-time cargo tracking, and logistics insurance. Reducing transport incidents by even one per warehouse per year across the network represents a substantial recovery in supply capacity.

Recommendation 2 — Launch a systematic warehouse quality upgrade programme. The strong positive relationship between government certification grade and shipment volume provides a clear ROI calculation for quality investment. Priority should be given to the approximately 6,400 Grade C warehouses, where upgrades would yield the highest incremental volume gains. Targeted infrastructure investment in temperature regulation machinery should accompany certification upgrades.

Recommendation 3 — Use the model for quarterly shipment planning immediately. Despite the modest R² of 0.27, the model's test RMSE of 9,897 tons is significantly better than the current approach of uniform or approximation-based allocation. Deploying the XGBoost model as a quarterly planning tool will reduce both stockouts in high-demand warehouses and excess inventory in low-demand ones.

Recommendation 4 — Target marketing investment in high-breakdown, high-volume warehouses. Since breakdown frequency is a proxy for operational intensity and high demand, warehouses with consistently high wh_breakdown_l3m scores are the natural candidates for targeted advertising campaigns in their catchment areas — these regions already demonstrate strong underlying demand.

Recommendation 5 — Collect richer data to improve the model in the next iteration. The 73% unexplained variance strongly suggests that consumer demand signals, seasonality data, competitor pricing, and promotional spend data should be incorporated in the next model version. These additions have the potential to push model performance into a substantially more useful range for operational deployment.

                linewidth=1.5, label=f'Mean Error: {residuals.mean():,.0f} tons')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Residual (Actual − Predicted) in Tons', fontsize=11)
axes[0].set_ylabel('Frequency', fontsize=11)
axes[0].set_title('Figure 12a: Residual Distribution', fontsize=12)
axes[0].legend()

# Residuals vs Predicted scatter
axes[1].scatter(y_pred_final, residuals, alpha=0.3, color='steelblue', s=10)
axes[1].axhline(0, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5)
axes[1].set_xlabel('Predicted Shipment Weight (Tons)', fontsize=11)
axes[1].set_ylabel('Residual (Tons)', fontsize=11)
axes[1].set_title('Figure 12b: Residuals vs Predicted Values', fontsize=12)

plt.suptitle('Figure 12: Residual Analysis — XGBoost (Tuned)', fontsize=13, y=1.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('residual_analysis.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()
print("Figure 12 saved.")

# Print residual statistics
print(f"\nResidual Statistics:")
print(f"  Mean  : {residuals.mean():,.2f} tons  (ideal = 0)")
print(f"  Std   : {residuals.std():,.2f} tons")
print(f"  Min   : {residuals.min():,.2f} tons")
print(f"  Max   : {residuals.max():,.2f} tons")

# ── 3. Model Comparison Bar Chart ────────────────────────────────────────────
model_names = [
    'OLS Baseline', 'Decision Tree', 'Bagging', 'XGBoost\n(Default)',
    'Random Forest\n(Default)', 'AdaBoost', 'Gradient Boosting\n(Default)',
    'Random Forest\n(Tuned)', 'Gradient Boosting\n(Tuned)', 'XGBoost\n(Tuned)'
]
test_rmse_values = [
    10379.41, 14390.93, 10596.95, 10352.70,
    10152.37, 10076.94, 9909.22,
    9914.08, 9904.62, 9896.62
]

colors = ['#aec7e8'] * 9 + ['#d62728']  # highlight best model in red

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 6))
bars = ax.bar(model_names, test_rmse_values, color=colors, edgecolor='white', width=0.6)

# Baseline reference line
ax.axhline(10379.41, color='navy', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.2,
           label=f'OLS Baseline: 10,379 tons')

# Value labels on bars
for bar, val in zip(bars, test_rmse_values):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2, bar.get_height() + 50,
            f'{val:,.0f}', ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=8.5)

ax.set_ylabel('Test RMSE (Tons)', fontsize=11)
ax.set_title('Figure 13: Test RMSE Comparison — All Models', fontsize=13, pad=12)
ax.set_ylim(8000, 15500)
ax.legend(fontsize=10)
plt.xticks(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('model_comparison.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')

Write-up for Figures 11, 12, and 13 (add to Section 7 of report)


Figure 11 — Actual vs Predicted


The scatter plot shows predictions tracking actuals reasonably well in the low-to-mid range (2,000–30,000 tons), with points clustering near the perfect prediction line in that zone. However, above 30,000 tons the model systematically under-predicts — predictions plateau around 25,000–30,000 tons even as actuals extend to 55,000 tons. This compression at the upper tail is characteristic of gradient boosted tree models when high-value observations are sparse in training data. It confirms the model is well-calibrated for typical warehouses but less reliable for the highest-volume outliers.

---

Figure 12 — Residual Analysis


Two important findings emerge. First, the residual distribution (Figure 12a) is centred at just −21 tons — effectively zero — confirming the model has no systematic directional bias. The shape is approximately bell-curved, indicating errors are largely random. Second, Figure 12b (residuals vs predicted) reveals a funnel pattern: residuals are tightly clustered at low predicted values but spread widely at higher predicted values. This is heteroscedasticity — the model is more uncertain about high-volume warehouses than low-volume ones. This is consistent with the actual vs predicted finding and suggests that future model iterations should explore log-transforming the target variable to stabilise variance.

---

Figure 13 — Model Comparison Bar Chart


The bar chart visually confirms the progression from baseline to final model. Decision Tree is a clear outlier at 14,391 tons due to complete overfitting. All tuned models fall below the OLS baseline (dashed line at 10,379 tons), with XGBoost (Tuned) achieving the lowest test RMSE of 9,897 tons — highlighted in red as the selected final model. The three tuned models are nearly indistinguishable visually, reinforcing that the dataset has a genuine performance ceiling with the current feature set.
